summary.text: Stars and bars is a graphical aid for deriving combinatorial theorems, also called sticks and stones or balls and bars.
It solves counting problems such as how many ways n indistinguishable balls can be put into k distinguishable bins.
With two balls and three bins, each string holds two stars and two bars, since two bars separate three bins.

facts.label: Other names
facts.value: Sticks and stones, balls and bars, dots and dividers

facts.label: Bars needed
facts.value: Separating k bins takes k − 1 bars placed between stars

facts.label: Slots per layout
facts.value: n + k − 1 slots, with k − 1 of them holding bars

facts.label: Gaps between stars
facts.value: With n stars there are n − 1 gaps where a bar may go

facts.label: Physics use
facts.value: Ehrenfest and Kamerlingh Onnes used it to derive Planck's count of complexions

items.prompt: You lay 10 marbles in a row and want to drop them into 4 labelled boxes with no box left empty, using dividers placed between marbles. How many different gaps could hold a divider?

options.label: 8 gaps
10 gaps
11 gaps
9 gaps

items.explain: With n objects in a row there are n − 1 gaps between them, so 10 marbles leave 9 places for a bar, and no gap takes more than one bar.

items.prompt: You want to split a row of marbles into 4 labelled boxes by laying dividers between them. How many dividers do you need?

options.label: Four, one for each box
Three, one fewer than the boxes
Five, to also mark both ends
Two, one for each pair of boxes

items.explain: Separating k bins takes k − 1 bars, just as two bars separate three bins.

items.prompt: Each of 3 boxes must hold at least one marble. Could two dividers sit side by side with no marble between them?

options.label: No, because that would leave a box empty
Yes, as long as the marbles are identical
Yes, if the dividers are at the far ends
No, because dividers must always alternate with boxes

items.explain: When no bin may be empty, there is at most one bar between any two stars, so bars never touch.

items.prompt: Three identical coins go into two numbered pockets. What tells two arrangements apart?

options.label: Which particular coins are in which pocket
The order in which the coins were dropped in
Only the number of coins in each pocket
Only which pocket holds the most coins

items.explain: The objects cannot be told apart but the bins can, so configurations differ only by how many objects each bin holds.

items.prompt: Every jar must get at least one of 7 marbles. How can you turn this into a problem where jars may also be empty?

options.label: Add one extra marble to every jar before counting
Lower each jar's count by one and let jars be empty
Remove the labels so the jars cannot be told apart
Count the layouts twice, once for each jar order

items.explain: Requiring positive amounts is the same as shifting each amount down by one and then only requiring them to be non-negative.

items.prompt: Four balls go into three bins, drawn as a row of 6 symbols: 4 stars and 2 bars. What do you choose to fix one layout?

options.label: Which 2 of the 6 slots hold the bars
Which 4 balls go into the first bin
Which of the 3 bins gets the first star
Which 6 symbols are placed first

items.explain: Lay out n + k − 1 slots and choose k − 1 of them for the bars, or equivalently choose n for the stars.

paragraphs.heading: A picture for counting
paragraphs.text: Stars and bars is a picture-based aid for deriving certain results in combinatorics. Other names for it include dots and dividers, balls and bars, and sticks and stones. It answers counting questions like this one: in how many ways can n identical balls be put into k bins that can be told apart? The method is often introduced to prove two basic theorems about how many solutions an equation has.

paragraphs.heading: Drawing the bins
paragraphs.text: Because the objects are all alike, an arrangement is fixed only by how many objects land in each numbered bin. Draw the n objects as a row of stars, and mark the boundary between neighbouring bins with a bar. Separating k bins takes k − 1 bars. With two balls and three bins, for example, every picture has two stars and two bars.

paragraphs.heading: No empty bins
paragraphs.text: In the first theorem, every bin must hold at least one object. Then at most one bar can sit between any two stars. A row of n stars has n − 1 gaps, so the task is to choose k − 1 of those gaps for bars. That makes the number of lists of k positive integers adding up to n equal to the count of subsets of size k − 1 taken from a set with n − 1 elements.

paragraphs.heading: Empty bins allowed
paragraphs.text: In the second theorem, bins may be empty, so each count only has to be non-negative. Bars can now sit side by side, and they can also go before the first star or after the last. Set out n + k − 1 places in a row; picking which k − 1 of them hold bars, or equally which n hold stars, fixes the arrangement. Here the picture can even have more bars than stars, which cannot happen when no bin is empty.

paragraphs.heading: One theorem from the other
paragraphs.text: The first theorem can be recast as the second. Shift each variable down by 1, and the demand that each be positive becomes the demand that each be non-negative. For a fixed k, the counts for n = 0, 1, 2, 3 and onward run along the (k − 1)st diagonal of Pascal's triangle. With k = 3 they are the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, found on the second diagonal.

paragraphs.heading: A use in physics
paragraphs.text: The same picture turned up in physics. Paul Ehrenfest and Heike Kamerlingh Onnes used it, writing ε where a star would go and 0 where a bar would go, to derive Max Planck's count of complexions for resonators of a single frequency. Their example had N = 4 and P = 7, giving R = 120 combinations. They wrote the 4-tuple (4, 2, 0, 1) as εεεε0εε00ε.
